q: Which description of an RLS policy in PostgreSQL is most accurate?
options: A trigger that copies allowed rows into a separate private table
A rule in the app code that removes rows after the query returns
A filter condition the database adds to queries automatically
A view that each developer must call instead of the base table
explanation: A policy acts like a silent WHERE clause that the engine adds to every query from the affected roles, so no application code has to change.

q: Why do prepared statements stop SQL Injection?
options: The database removes all quote characters from the input
The query structure is fixed before the user values arrive
The query runs with superuser rights, so no errors can occur
The user input is encrypted before it is sent to the server
explanation: The SQL template is parsed first and the query tree is locked. Values sent later are treated only as literal data, so they cannot change the logic of the query.

q: One RLS policy on rental uses the condition staff_id = (SELECT staff_id FROM staff WHERE username = current_user). Why does this single policy show Mike only his rentals and Jon only his rentals?
options: The application adds a WHERE clause for each user before it sends the query
The policy is rebuilt by the DBA each time a different staff member logs in
current_user is read per session, so each user gets a different filter
Postgres makes one copy of the rental table for every member of store_clerk
explanation: current_user returns the role of the current database session, so the same policy expression produces a different filter for each logged-in user. No application code or extra policies are needed.

q: The DVD store website hides all SQL error messages. An attacker sends customer_id=5 AND 1=1 and then customer_id=5 AND 1=2. In this Boolean-based blind SQLi, what signal does the attacker rely on?
options: A copy of the database backup left on the server
Detailed SQL error messages printed on the web page
Differences in the page content for TRUE vs FALSE
The exact time the server takes to send a reply
explanation: Boolean-based blind SQLi asks TRUE/FALSE questions and reads the answer from how the page changes (profile loads vs. profile disappears). No error messages are needed.

q: In modern PostgreSQL (since 8.1), what is the relationship between a "user" and a "group"?
options: Groups can log in, but users can only receive privileges
Both are roles; a user is simply a role with LOGIN
Users are stored in tables; groups are stored in files
They are separate objects that cannot be linked together
explanation: Users and groups were merged into one concept: ROLE. A role with LOGIN acts as a user; a role without LOGIN that other roles are members of acts as a group.

q: Which command is equivalent to CREATE USER alice WITH PASSWORD 'x';?
options: CREATE ROLE alice WITH NOLOGIN PASSWORD 'x';
CREATE ROLE alice WITH LOGIN PASSWORD 'x';
CREATE GROUP alice WITH INHERIT PASSWORD 'x';
CREATE ROLE alice WITH SUPERUSER PASSWORD 'x';
explanation: CREATE USER is the same as CREATE ROLE, except that LOGIN is added by default.

q: RLS is enabled on rental, with a policy that applies only to store_clerk. The DBA connects as postgres (superuser) and runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rental;. What happens?
options: It fails, because RLS blocks every role except store_clerk
It counts all rows, because superusers always bypass RLS
It returns only the rows whose staff_id is equal to 1
It returns zero rows, because postgres has no matching policy
explanation: Superusers (and roles with BYPASSRLS) always bypass row-level security, so the count includes every row. This is another reason why apps must never connect as postgres.

q: Which statement best describes Second-Order SQL Injection?
options: The attacker uses two different users to log in at once
The attack is sent twice to make sure that the server accepts it
The payload runs at once in the first query that reads it
The payload is stored first and runs later in another query
explanation: In second-order SQLi the payload is stored safely first (e.g. as a last name), then executed later when another part of the system reads it and concatenates it into a new query.

q: What is the root cause of SQL Injection?
options: The tables do not have primary keys or indexes
The database engine has a bug in its own SQL parser
User input is mixed into SQL code as plain text
The server runs an outdated PostgreSQL version
explanation: SQL Injection is an application-level flaw: raw user input is concatenated into the SQL string, so the engine cannot tell data apart from code.

q: In which situation would an attacker choose time-based blind SQLi (for example, using pg_sleep(10)) instead of Boolean-based blind SQLi?
options: When the page looks the same for TRUE and FALSE
When the attacker already knows the admin password
When the website shows full SQL errors to visitors
When the database uses the Serializable isolation level
explanation: When the page is identical for TRUE and FALSE, there is no visual clue. The attacker then uses response time as the signal: a 10-second delay means the condition was TRUE.

q: An AI pre-processing script reads actor names from the actor table and builds an UPDATE statement with a Python f-string. Which statement is true?
options: Data from your own tables is safe because it was checked on insert
Only data from web forms needs parameters, not data from tables
f-strings are safe in Python because they escape quotes by default
Data from your own tables can still carry an injection payload
explanation: Golden rule: never fully trust data, even from your own tables. A stored value can carry a payload that runs when it is concatenated into a new query (second-order SQLi). f-strings do no escaping.

q: The store_clerk role was never granted DELETE on rental. A DBA then runs: REVOKE DELETE ON rental FROM store_clerk; What is the effect of this command?
options: It blocks DELETE even when a member gets DELETE in another way
It raises an error, so the rest of the script stops running
It has no effect, since PostgreSQL has no explicit deny rule
It removes the store_clerk role from all of its member users
explanation: PostgreSQL privileges are additive; there is no "deny" entry. REVOKE only removes a privilege that was granted. If it was never granted, nothing changes, and a member could still get DELETE through a direct grant or another role.

q: According to the Principle of Least Privilege, why is it dangerous to connect a web app or AI pipeline using the postgres account?
options: The postgres account cannot run SELECT on normal tables
The postgres account is not allowed to use prepared statements
Superuser connections are slower than normal connections
A single SQL injection gives the attacker full control
explanation: If the app connects as a superuser, any SQL Injection inherits superuser power: the attacker can drop databases, read local files or even run OS commands.

q: Which limitation of traditional RBAC does Row-Level Security solve?
options: RBAC cannot control INSERT, only SELECT and DELETE commands
RBAC only works when the app uses an ORM such as SQLAlchemy
RBAC cannot give the same privilege to more than one user at once
RBAC controls table access, not which rows a user can see
explanation: RBAC works at the table level (can this user access the table?). RLS answers a finer question: which specific rows can this user access?

q: A DBA runs ALTER TABLE rental ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; but forgets to create any policy. store_clerk still has SELECT on rental. What does a normal (non-owner) member of store_clerk get from SELECT * FROM rental;?
options: Only rows where staff_id is NULL, as a safe default value
All rows, because RLS only starts working once a policy exists
No rows, because RLS denies access when no policy matches
An error, because a table with RLS must have a policy first
explanation: When RLS is enabled and no policy applies, PostgreSQL uses a default-deny rule: no rows are visible, and no error is raised.

q: Under PostgreSQL's default isolation level, which anomaly may still occur between two reads in the same transaction?
options: Dirty reads of uncommitted updates
Non-repeatable reads after another transaction commits
Uncommitted data becoming durable
All transactions appearing serial
explanation: Read Committed prevents dirty reads but permits non-repeatable reads, as the recap states.

q: An attacker changes labels in an AI training table before a model is retrained. Which risk is illustrated?
options: Index fragmentation
Transaction deadlock
Data poisoning
Query-plan instability
explanation: Manipulated training labels can contaminate the data used to train the model.

q: In the slide's vulnerable staff-login example, what is the combined purpose of OR 1=1 and the SQL comment marker?
options: Force the predicate true and comment out the password condition
Encrypt the username and escape the password
Create a new staff role and revoke its password
Delay execution and trigger an error message
explanation: The tautology makes the condition true, and the comment suppresses the remaining password predicate.

q: What role does the single quote in an injected username play in the vulnerable login query?
options: It grants SELECT on staff
It requests an implicit transaction
It invokes a PostgreSQL function
It closes the surrounding SQL string literal
explanation: The quote escapes the intended data string, allowing subsequent input to be interpreted as SQL syntax.

q: A page loads when an injected condition is TRUE and disappears when FALSE. What could an attacker infer by repeatedly changing a substring test?
options: The database engine's physical index layout
Secret text one character at a time
The duration of database checkpoints
The number of open transactions
explanation: The slide shows substring(version(),1,1) as an example of character-by-character inference.

q: A site returns identical page content for TRUE and FALSE. Which observation can still carry information about an injected condition?
options: Whether an index is visible in pgAdmin
Whether a trigger definition was updated
A reproducible response-time delay
A change to the application's CSS
explanation: Time-based blind SQLi uses conditional delay as a side channel when content gives no clue.

q: In the lecture example, what is the purpose of testing current_user in a conditional delay?
options: To discover the database role used by the connection
To change the active user's password
To grant access to the payment table
To list every role in the cluster
explanation: The example conditions the delay on whether current_user is postgres, revealing the connection role through timing.

q: A malicious surname is stored safely but later appended to a reporting query. At which stage does the SQL Injection vulnerability become exploitable?
options: When an index is created for surname
When the string is inserted using safe parameters
When the database takes a backup
When the reporting query mixes the stored value into SQL text
explanation: Second-order SQLi arises when previously stored content is later treated as executable SQL.

q: An AI pipeline reads actor names from a trusted-looking database table. Which coding change best addresses the lecture's second-order SQLi risk?
options: Use a larger VARCHAR field
Build an UPDATE with f-string formatting
Bind actor names as query parameters when issuing UPDATE
Disable all indexes on the actor table
explanation: Stored strings are not inherently safe; parameter binding prevents actor names from modifying the UPDATE statement structure.

q: In PREPARE staff_login(text, text), what do $1 and $2 represent?
options: Column positions in the staff table
Parameter placeholders populated at execution time
The first two rows returned by the query
Two role identifiers granted LOGIN
explanation: The prepared query uses placeholders for username and password, with values bound later at EXECUTE.

q: A malicious username contains quote characters and OR 1=1, but is sent as a bound parameter. What happens to the query's intended predicate?
options: It is replaced with an always-true expression
It becomes a new SQL comment
It is executed as an independent statement
It remains unchanged because the payload is treated as data
explanation: The prepared statement's SQL structure is fixed; the payload is treated as a literal username value.

q: A search endpoint expects customer_id to be an integer. Which additional application-layer control matches the slide's guidance?
options: Validate that customer_id has an integer type before querying
Grant the application SUPERUSER temporarily
Use string concatenation only for numeric inputs
Allow all customer_id values and rely on hidden errors
explanation: Input validation should enforce integer types for customer_id in addition to parameterized queries.

q: Which combination most closely reflects the defense-in-depth approach in the lecture?
options: Only remove database error messages
Only assign a password to the postgres role
Use parameterized queries, input validation, and least-privilege connections
Make all tables read-only for the database owner
explanation: The slide combines ORM/prepared statement use, validation, and least privilege rather than relying on a single layer.

q: An inference service only reads feature records. Under PoLP, which account configuration is most appropriate?
options: A superuser account so queries never fail
A restricted role with only the required read privileges
A role with CREATE ROLE and DROP permissions
A table owner account with unrestricted write access
explanation: The Principle of Least Privilege requires only the minimum access needed for the service to function.

q: What is the immediate effect of CREATE ROLE data_analyst; as written in the lecture?
options: It creates a role without LOGIN by default
It creates a role that can log in automatically
It creates a database named data_analyst
It grants SELECT on all public tables
explanation: CREATE ROLE defaults to NOLOGIN, so the example acts as a group-style role.

q: Why does RBAC usually assign privileges to group roles before users?
options: It automatically turns RLS off
It replaces the need for table grants
It forces all users to share one password
It centralizes permission management for multiple users
explanation: Permissions can be granted once to the role and reused via membership by Mike, Jon, and others.

q: Which command adds jon to the existing store_clerk role?
options: GRANT jon TO store_clerk;
GRANT store_clerk TO jon;
ALTER ROLE store_clerk OWNER TO jon;
CREATE USER store_clerk FOR jon;
explanation: GRANT store_clerk TO jon assigns membership in the group role to Jon.

q: A DBA wants to remove Jon's membership in store_clerk without deleting either role. Which command matches the lecture?
options: DROP ROLE jon;
REVOKE jon FROM store_clerk;
REVOKE store_clerk FROM jon;
DROP OWNED BY store_clerk;
explanation: Role membership is removed by revoking the granted group role from the member.

q: Which SQL command grants clerks permission to read film records without allowing film changes?
options: GRANT SELECT ON film TO store_clerk;
GRANT INSERT ON film TO store_clerk;
GRANT UPDATE ON film TO store_clerk;
GRANT ALL ON film TO store_clerk;
explanation: SELECT permits reading; INSERT and UPDATE change data, while ALL grants broader permissions.

q: According to the lecture's RBAC setup, which privilege set is granted on rental to store_clerk?
options: SELECT and DELETE
INSERT and DELETE
UPDATE and DELETE
SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE
explanation: The rental grant includes SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, while DELETE is not granted.

q: Mike and Jon both inherit SELECT ON rental from store_clerk. Without RLS, what is the relevant privacy problem?
options: Only the role creator can query rental
Each clerk can read rentals belonging to the other clerk
Membership revokes SELECT from both users
The database copies rental into separate tables
explanation: Table-level RBAC permits access to the table, not different subsets of its rows.

q: Why is RLS especially useful for a multi-tenant application sharing one table?
options: It eliminates every need for application authentication
It guarantees queries use index scans
It restricts which rows each tenant's role can access
It encrypts every row with a different key
explanation: RLS applies database-enforced row filters so tenants can share tables while maintaining data isolation.

q: Which sequence correctly implements the basic two-step RLS approach?
options: Enable RLS on a table, then create a policy for permitted rows
Create an index, then update the table's owner
Create separate tables per user, then hide the originals
Revoke LOGIN from every user, then enable autocommit
explanation: The lecture first enables row-level security and then defines a policy that controls visibility.

q: In CREATE POLICY ... FOR ALL TO store_clerk USING (...), which clause identifies the roles covered by the policy?
options: USING
FOR ALL
ON rental
TO store_clerk
explanation: TO selects the role or roles to which the policy applies; USING provides the row filter.

q: What does FOR ALL signify in the slide's rental policy definition?
options: The policy ignores row filters
The policy targets all four command categories named in the slide
The policy grants ALL table privileges
The policy applies to every database in the cluster
explanation: The slide explicitly explains FOR ALL as applying to SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE policy behavior.

q: Which condition is used in the rental policy to match a row to the currently active staff role?
options: rental_id = current_user
customer_id = current_user
staff_id = (SELECT staff_id FROM staff WHERE username = current_user)
staff_id IS NOT NULL
explanation: The policy looks up the staff_id for the current database role and compares it with each rental row's staff_id.

q: After SET ROLE mike, why can SELECT * FROM rental return Mike's records without a manual WHERE clause?
options: The database applies the matching RLS policy automatically
SET ROLE physically deletes Jon's rows
PostgreSQL creates a materialized view for Mike
The application adds a special staff filter
explanation: PostgreSQL automatically enforces the policy condition when the query runs in Mike's role context.

q: In Lab 1, which table permissions should cashier_role have on payment?
options: SELECT only
INSERT and UPDATE only
SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE
SELECT and INSERT
explanation: Lab 1 requires SELECT and INSERT on payment; UPDATE and DELETE are not part of this grant.

q: Which statement grants cashier_role read access to both film and staff in the lecture's solution?
options: GRANT SELECT ON payment TO cashier_role;
GRANT SELECT ON film, staff TO cashier_role;
GRANT SELECT ON DATABASE dvdrental TO cashier_role;
GRANT ALL ON film, staff TO cashier_role;
explanation: The lab's solution grants SELECT on both named tables in one command.

q: In the payment isolation lab, which table is the target of ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY?
options: staff
rental
payment
film
explanation: Lab 2 enables RLS on the payment table to restrict each cashier's payment visibility.

q: Which RLS command scope is used for isolate_cashier_payments in the solution?
options: FOR SELECT TO cashier_role
FOR ALL TO PUBLIC
FOR UPDATE TO store_manager
FOR INSERT TO postgres
explanation: The solution creates a SELECT policy that applies to cashier_role specifically.

q: According to the Lab 2 solution, which output pair corresponds to SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payment under SET ROLE mike and SET ROLE jon?
options: Mike: 0; Jon: 0
explanation: The slide reports 7292 visible payments for Mike and 7304 for Jon after switching roles.

q: Which set best represents the three database-security pillars emphasized at the end of Session 7?
options: Indexing, sharding, and replication
Prevent SQLi, enforce least privilege, and isolate rows with RLS
Autocommit, write-ahead logging, and vacuum
Partitioning, hashing, and sorting
explanation: The final takeaways bring together SQLi prevention, RBAC/least privilege, and RLS.

q: A student deploys an AI model backed by PostgreSQL. Which implementation choice best applies the session's project guidance?
options: Connect with postgres to simplify administration
Keep all features in a publicly writable table
Use a restricted application role and parameterized database access
Disable all user roles and manage security in CSS
explanation: The project integration slide promotes applying database security practices in a real AI application rather than relying on a superuser connection.
